SQL · my own queries

1. Product & Customer Performance Analysis

Practice project applying core SQL to sales data. I used a free online SQL editor (SQLite), so the dataset is small by design: an orders table (8 orders) and a customers table linked by customer_id. The sample data was generated by ChatGPT.

Q1 · Revenue and orders by product

SELECT product, SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue,
       COUNT(order_id) AS total_order
FROM orders
GROUP BY product;
productrevenueorders
Shoes2,2504
Bag6502
Hat3502

Q2 · High-value vs low-value orders (revenue ≥ 500)

SELECT
  CASE WHEN revenue >= 500 THEN 'High Value'
       ELSE 'Low Value' END AS order_type,
  SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue,
  COUNT(order_id) AS total_order
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_type;
typerevenueorders
High Value1,8503
Low Value1,4005

Q3 · Orders, revenue and average order value by city

SELECT c.city, COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_order,
       SUM(o.revenue) AS total_revenue,
       AVG(o.revenue) AS avg_order_value
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;
cityordersrevenueavg
HCM31,600533
Hanoi2950475
Can Tho1350350
Da Nang2350175

Key insights

  • Shoes are the top product: 2,250 of 3,250 in total revenue (~69%) from 4 of the 8 orders.
  • 3 high-value orders bring in 1,850 (~57% of revenue), more than the 5 low-value orders combined (1,400).
  • Ho Chi Minh City leads with 1,600 in revenue (~49%) from 3 orders; no other city passes 950.
  • Average order value varies widely by city (for example, Hanoi ~475 vs Da Nang ~175).

Next step: repeat these queries on a larger dataset using a local database (SQLite, MySQL, or PostgreSQL are free).

Power BI · guided project

2. Data Professional Survey Analysis

Analyze a survey of data professionals (630 responses) to understand job roles, salary, favorite programming languages, and job satisfaction. Built by following this YouTube tutorial; the dataset comes from the video.

What I did

  • Cleaned and transformed the data in Power Query: split columns, removed unneeded columns, replaced values, changed data types, and added a custom column converting salary ranges into one value (midpoint).
  • Built a one-page interactive dashboard: respondents by country, average salary by job title, favorite programming language by job title, difficulty of entering the data field, and satisfaction gauges for work-life balance and salary.

Key insights

  • Data Scientists have the highest average salary, followed by Data Engineers (based on salary-range midpoints; only 25 and 38 of the 630 respondents, so treat as indicative).
  • Python is the favorite programming language overall (420 of 630 respondents).
  • Work-life balance satisfaction (~5.74/10) is higher than salary satisfaction (~4.27/10).
  • About one-third (32%) found it difficult or very difficult to break into data; the largest group (43%) was neutral.

Takeaways for people entering data

  • Python is a core skill worth prioritizing for Data Analysts.
  • Structured learning paths can help reduce the barrier to entry.
Excel · guided project

3. Customer Purchase Behavior Analysis

Find which customer factors relate to buying a bike: income and gender, age group, and commute distance (~1,000 records). Built by following this YouTube tutorial; the dataset comes from the video.

What I did

  • Cleaned data: removed 26 duplicate records (1,026 → 1,000 rows), changed M/S to Married/Single, F/M to Female/Male and “10+ Miles” to “More than 10 Miles”, and created an age-group column.
  • Analyzed with Pivot Tables: average income and purchases by gender, purchases by commute distance, purchases by age group.
  • Built a dashboard with charts and slicers (marital status, education, region).

Purchase rate by commute distance

0–1 mile54.6%
1–2 miles45.6%
2–5 miles58.6%
5–10 miles39.6%
10+ miles29.7%

Purchase rate by age group

Ages 25–3035.5%
Ages 31–5454.6%
Ages 55+31.2%

Key insights

  • Middle-aged customers (31–54) are the most active buyers: 383 of 481 buyers (80%) and a 54.6% purchase rate.
  • Gender: purchase rates are almost equal (female 48.9%, male 47.4%); male customers have higher average income (58,063 vs 54,581).
  • Distance: the purchase rate peaks at 2–5 miles and 0–1 mile, then falls beyond 5 miles. Most buyers live within 1 mile (42%) simply because that is the largest group (366 customers).

Takeaways

  • Focus marketing on the middle-aged segment.
  • Do not target by gender, since purchase rates are nearly the same; customers living over 5 miles away buy less often, so improving access for them is worth testing.
